MDR/XDR A. baumannii Analysis with Environmental Co-Selection

This comprehensive gene-centric report analyzes 145 A. baumannii genomes with focus on carbapenem resistance, colistin resistance, biofilm formation, and environmental co-selection markers. Each gene is shown with ALL genomes that contain it for easy tracking of resistance spread.

NEW: Dynamic grouping by typing (ST, K, OCL, capsule) and gene co‑occurrence analysis.

⚠️ Critical Resistance Alert

43 carbapenemase genes detected across samples. Carbapenem-resistant A. baumannii (CRAB) is a WHO Critical Priority pathogen.

⚠️ Environmental Co-Selection Alert

176 environmental resistance markers detected. These genes can co-select for antibiotic resistance in hospital environments.

Population Structure Overview

This table summarises the key typing results for each genome. Understanding the population structure helps identify dominant clones, track outbreaks, and link genotypes to phenotypes.

  • MLST (Sequence Type): Gold standard for global epidemiology.
  • Capsule Typing (K:OCL): K (capsule) and OCL (lipooligosaccharide) loci are critical for virulence and immune evasion.
  • ND: Not Determined.

MLST Typing – Acknowledgments & Licensing
MLST scheme powered by Prof. Torsten Seemann's Perl scripts and the PubMLST database (Jolley et al., Wellcome Open Res 2018).
Note: Due to recent licensing changes and the new PubMLST data policy, the allele definitions used in this report are current as of 2024. Future updates may require manual downloads from the PubMLST website.
We are grateful to the PubMLST curators and Torsten Seemann for providing these essential open‑source tools.

MLST Analysis - Dual Scheme (Pasteur & Oxford)

Multi‑Locus Sequence Typing (MLST) uses internal fragments of seven housekeeping genes. It is highly reproducible and defines Sequence Types (STs). Closely related STs belong to the same Clonal Complex (CC).

21 unique Pasteur STs and 18 Oxford STs identified. International Clone (IC) classification helps track global lineages.

Kaptive Capsule Typing – Acknowledgments
Kaptive3 developed by Stanton et al. (Mgen. 2025;11(6):001428) Identifies capsule (K) and lipooligosaccharide (OCL) loci in Acinetobacter baumannii from whole‑genome sequence data.
We are deeply grateful to the developers for making this tool freely available for genomic surveillance of A. baumannii.

Capsule Typing (Kaptive) Analysis

Kaptive identifies capsule (K) and lipooligosaccharide (OCL) loci in A. baumannii. The capsule is a major virulence determinant, protecting against phagocytosis and complement killing. Specific K types are associated with different clonal complexes and clinical outcomes. OCL (O-Chain Locus) influences immune evasion and serum resistance.

AMR Detection Tools & Databases
ABRicate by Prof. Torsten Seemann Powered by databases: CARD, ARG-ANNOT, NCBI AMR, MEGARes, ResFinder
AMRFinderPlus by NCBI Comprehensive resistance gene and point mutation detection.
We are deeply grateful to all developers and curators for their open‑source contributions.
⚠️ Important Caveat: Gene presence does not necessarily imply phenotypic resistance. Confirmation by antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) is required for clinical decisions. The term "CRAB" (carbapenem-resistant A. baumannii) used in this report is based solely on the detection of carbapenemase genes; clinical correlation with MIC values is essential.

🔬 Understanding Database-Specific Gene Reporting

Why do I see the same gene reported by multiple databases?

AcinetoScope uses 10 different databases because no single database is comprehensive. Each has unique strengths and limitations.

  • CARD – Strict SNP-based cutoffs; excellent for precise allele identification.
  • ResFinder – Highly sensitive; appends _1 to primary allele variants (e.g., blaOXA-23_1 → same as blaOXA-23).
  • MEGARes – Optimised for metagenomics; includes biocide and metal resistance.
  • AMRFinderPlus – NCBI gold standard; includes point mutations.
  • VFDB – Comprehensive virulence factor database.
  • BacMet2 – Biocide and heavy metal resistance genes.

💡 How to interpret duplicate entries:

  • High confidence – Gene found in 3+ databases.
  • Moderate confidence – Gene found in 2 databases.
  • Low confidence – Gene found in only 1 database; may be a database-specific artifact.
  • ⚠️ ResFinder naming: _1 suffix (e.g., blaOXA-23_1) indicates the primary allele variant — it is the same gene as blaOXA-23.
  • ⚠️ Intrinsic vs Acquired: Genes like blaOXA-66 and blaOXA-69 are intrinsic OXA-51-like genes in A. baumannii and do not indicate acquired carbapenem resistance. Users are encouraged to consult the literature for gene-specific context.

Pro tip: The Database column shows exactly which database found each gene. Use this to assess confidence and identify database-specific artifacts. No results are merged or filtered — we preserve all findings for full transparency.

🗃️ Database Roles & Reporting Logic

AcinetoScope uses multiple databases to maximise sensitivity and specificity. Each database is kept separate in the report to preserve provenance and allow users to assess confidence.

🟢 CARD

Strengths: Strict SNP-based cutoffs, curated protein families.
Limitations: May miss novel variants.
Reporting: Precise allele assignments.

🔵 ResFinder

Strengths: Highly sensitive for known resistance genes.
Limitations: May misclassify alleles (e.g., blaADC-25 false positives).
Reporting: Appends _1 to primary allele variants.

🟠 MEGARes

Strengths: Includes biocide and metal resistance genes.
Limitations: Less focused on clinical AMR.
Reporting: Functional metagenomic annotations.

🔴 AMRFinderPlus

Strengths: NCBI gold standard; includes point mutations.
Limitations: Slower to update with novel variants.
Reporting: Comprehensive AMR gene and mutation detection.

🩷 VFDB

Strengths: Comprehensive virulence factor database.
Limitations: Focused on virulence, not AMR.
Reporting: Virulence gene detection.

🤎 BacMet2

Strengths: Biocide and heavy metal resistance genes.
Limitations: Not focused on clinical AMR.
Reporting: Environmental co-selection markers.

🟣 ARG-ANNOT

Strengths: Broad AMR gene coverage.
Limitations: Older database, less frequently updated.
Reporting: AMR gene detection.

🔵 PlasmidFinder

Strengths: Generalist plasmid replicon detection.
Limitations: Not optimised for Acinetobacter.
Reporting: Plasmid replicon markers.

⚪ NCBI

Strengths: Broad general annotation.
Limitations: Not specialised for AMR or virulence.
Reporting: General gene annotation.

Why we keep results separate:

By preserving which database found each gene, users can:

  • Assess confidence — a gene found in 3+ databases is stronger evidence than one found in only 1.
  • Identify database-specific artifacts (e.g., ResFinder blaADC-25 false positives).
  • Understand differences in gene prevalence between databases.
  • Make informed decisions about which results to trust.

No results are merged or filtered — we present all findings transparently.

Virulence Detection Tools & Databases
ABRicate by Prof. Torsten Seemann Powered by the VFDB (Virulence Factor Database) – an open‑source resource for bacterial virulence factors.
We thank the VFDB curators and Prof. Seemann for their invaluable contributions.

Virulence Factors (Biofilm, Adhesion, Toxins)

Key A. baumannii virulence genes: biofilm formation (ompA, csu, bfmRS), pili, and iron uptake. Biofilm formation is critical for persistence on medical devices and hospital outbreaks. Use filters to explore specific mechanisms.

BACMET – Biocide & Heavy Metal Resistance
ABRicate by Prof. Torsten Seemann Powered by the BacMet database (Pal C, et al. Nucleic Acids Res. 2014;42:D737-43) – an open‑source resource for antibacterial biocide and metal resistance genes.
We thank the BacMet curators and Prof. Seemann for their invaluable contributions.

BACMET2 Database: Biocide & Heavy Metal Resistance

These genes confer resistance to disinfectants (quaternary ammonium, chlorhexidine) and heavy metals (mercury, copper, arsenic, etc.), which can co‑select for antibiotic resistance in hospital environments. Tracking these markers helps understand persistence and resistance spread.

AI Assistant Guide – Unleash the Power of AI for Genomic Epidemiology

This guide shows you how to leverage large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini to interact with your A. baumannii dataset – turning static reports into dynamic conversations.

Why Use AI for Genomic Data Analysis?

Modern AI models excel at:

  • Pattern recognition – spotting epidemiological trends, clone associations, and co‑occurrence networks.
  • Natural language queries – ask in plain English, get instant answers without writing code.
  • Hypothesis generation – uncover unexpected correlations that merit experimental follow‑up.
  • Literature synthesis – connect your findings with published resistance mechanisms and clinical guidelines.

Scientific note: AI is pattern‑finding, not causal‑inferring. Use it to suggest, then verify with wet‑lab or clinical correlation.

How to Feed This Report to AI

You have three powerful options:

  1. Upload the JSON file – genius_acinetobacter_ultimate_gene_centric_report.json contains all structured data. Upload it to ChatGPT (Advanced Data Analysis), Claude, or Gemini. Best for precise quantitative queries.
  2. Upload the HTML report – Modern AI tools can read HTML and extract tables. Upload the .html file directly – the AI will parse the tables and text. Great for visual context.
  3. Copy‑paste specific tables – If you only need a quick insight, copy a table (e.g., AMR gene list) and paste it into the chat. Instant, no file upload needed.

Pro tip: For best results, tell the AI: "You are a bioinformatician analysing A. baumannii genomes. The attached data contains typing, AMR, virulence, BACMET, and mutation information. Answer my questions with references to the data."

Scientifically Relevant Questions to Ask

🧬 Epidemiology & Clonality
  • What are the most common Pasteur STs in this dataset?
  • Which capsule types (K:OCL) are dominant?
  • Are there any ST‑capsule combinations with >2 isolates?
  • Which clones carry the most resistance genes?
💊 Antimicrobial Resistance
  • How many samples carry OXA-23? What are their STs?
  • Are there any NDM‑positive samples? What is their capsule type?
  • Which AMR genes co‑occur most frequently?
  • What is the distribution of colistin resistance genes (mcr, pmr)?
🦠 Virulence & Biofilm
  • Which samples carry biofilm genes (ompA, csu)?
  • List all isolates with the T6SS (tss, hcp).
  • Is there a correlation between capsule type and virulence gene carriage?
🧪 Mutations & Biocides
  • What are the most frequent point mutations in gyrA or parC?
  • Are there any 23S rRNA mutations (tigecycline resistance)?
  • Which samples carry qac genes (disinfectant resistance)?

Beyond tables: Ask the AI to “write a summary of the resistance profile for ST2” or “compare virulence gene carriage between K1 and K2 capsule types” – the report contains all data.

Scientific Rigour & Ethical AI Use

  • AI is your co‑pilot, not the pilot. Always interpret AI‑generated insights in the context of your local epidemiology, clinical guidelines, and laboratory validation.
  • Verify, verify, verify. Cross‑check critical calls (e.g., carbapenemase presence, colistin resistance) with primary literature, genome browsers, or secondary tools.
  • No patient‑identifiable data. Only upload aggregated, de‑identified genomic data. This report contains no clinical metadata.
  • Transparency in publications. If you use AI for exploratory analysis, mention it in the methods (e.g., “AI‑assisted pattern discovery was performed using a large language model, followed by manual curation”).
  • AI hallucination is real. If the AI confidently tells you that blaOXA-23 is found in E. coli or that tigecycline resistance is caused by a mutation in rpoB – don’t believe it. Treat every AI statement as a hypothesis, not a fact.

A (Mostly Serious) AI Survival Guide

  • If the AI says “I don’t know” – trust it. It’s being honest.
  • If the AI says “It is widely known” – ask for a reference. It may have made it up.
  • If the AI offers a completely novel evolutionary theory – check if your coffee is spiked.
  • Remember: AI won’t take your job – but a microbiologist who knows how to use AI might! So learn it, use it, and always keep a healthy dose of scepticism. 😉

Final thought: The best AI‑human partnership is one where the AI does the heavy pattern‑lifting, and you do the heavy thinking. Happy (and careful) exploring!

Antimicrobial resistance genes were identified using CARD [Alcock et al., 2023], ResFinder [Bortolaia et al., 2020], MEGARes 3.0 [Bonin et al., 2023], and ARG-ANNOT [Gupta et al., 2014]. For biocide and heavy metal resistance genes, BacMet [Pal et al., 2014] was used. Virulence screening was performed with ABRicate using VFDB [Chen et al., 2016]. Mutation detection was performed using AMRFinderPlus. FASTA QC was performed using Biopython [Cock et al., 2009]."

Funding & Support – Keeping the Lights On (with code and caffeine)

AcinetoScope is an independent, unfunded project born out of passion for genomic surveillance and AMR research at the University of Ghana Medical School.

No grants, no sponsors, no institutional backing – just a laptop, a lot of coffee, and a burning desire to help researchers fight antimicrobial resistance.
